newsitem.title: CHINA: China backs stock warning with tough penalties.
newsitem.headline: China backs stock warning with tough penalties.

text.p: China's tough penalties against banks and brokerages show market regulators are willing to back talk with action against improper stock trading, brokers and analysts said on Friday.
But although trading would remain cautious in the near term, investors still showed plenty of interest in buying shares, they said.

After the markets closed on Thursday, China punished Shenzhen Development Bank, the key blue chip on the nation's southern bourse in Shenzhen, by sacking its top official and seizing 90 million yuan ($10.8 million) in profits from trading in its own shares.
Beijing also dismissed the head of the Shanghai branch of the state-run Industrial and Commercial Bank of China for providing loans to securities companies for stock speculation.
The heads of three major securities firms were also dismissed for speculating in stocks.
"This shows the authorities are cracking down on securities-related crimes as hard as on other crimes," said a broker at China Guotai Securities in Shenzhen.
Shanghai and Shenzhen A shares for domestic investors fell sharply at the opening of trade on Friday but had clawed back all of the losses by midday.
Shanghai's A share index was up a modest 3.53 points at 1,269.37 while Shenzhen A shares added 5.31 points to 418.22.
The punitive measures followed last week's government ban on state banks speculating on the stock market and earlier moves to stop state enterprises and listed firms doing the same thing.
China has been trying to limit risk to the banking system by keeping bank funds out of the stock markets.
"Since they put these regulations in place, they had do to something to enforce them," said an analyst at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai.
But she added that investors were still keen to buy stocks and that some people took the early sell-off as an opportunity to pick up shares cheaply.
"The market has been aware of it (the punishments) for some time, so investors thought they might as well do a little bottom fishing," she said.
But the stock markets are expected to continue to be weak in the short term as state banks unwind their positions in line with the ban announced last Thursday, brokers said.
Banks were given 10 days to withdraw from the market.
The threat of a further crackdown if share prices moved up too sharply would cap the markets and keep prices within a narrow range through July, brokers said.
"Everyone's aware that there could be more measures in the pipeline, so they're just going to sit there," said the analyst at the foreign brokerage.

Before Beijing announced the measures to check speculation, many investors had bought shares on expectations that prices would climb as China prepared for the recovery of the British colony of Hong Kong on July 1.
Many investors had believed that Beijing would not want to risk political embarrassment with a clampdown on the domestic market ahead of the transfer of power.
But government regulators defied market expectations by starting their campaign to rein in prices in May.
